name: Complete Blood Count (CBC)
desc: Comprehensive panel measuring red blood cells, white blood cells, platelets, haemoglobin, haematocrit, and differential count. Used to diagnose anaemia, infections, bleeding disorders, polycythaemia, and haematological malignancies like leukaemia and lymphoma. One of the most frequently ordered diagnostic tests worldwide.

name: Haemoglobin (Hb)
desc: Measures concentration of haemoglobin in blood to detect and monitor anaemia, polycythaemia, and response to iron, B12, or folate therapy. Essential for pre-surgical screening, pregnancy anaemia monitoring, and chronic disease management such as CKD and thalassaemia carriers.

name: Peripheral Blood Smear (PBS)
desc: Microscopic examination of stained blood cells to identify abnormal morphology including sickle cells, target cells, blast cells, hypersegmented neutrophils, and malarial parasites. Critical for diagnosing haemolytic anaemias, thalassaemia, megaloblastic anaemia, and haematological malignancies such as CML, AML, and CLL.

name: ESR (Erythrocyte Sedimentation Rate)
desc: Measures rate at which red blood cells settle over one hour. Elevated ESR is a non-specific marker of systemic inflammation, infection, autoimmune disease, and malignancy. Commonly used to monitor disease activity in rheumatoid arthritis, tuberculosis, multiple myeloma, and temporal arteritis.

name: Reticulocyte Count
desc: Counts immature red blood cells to assess bone marrow erythropoietic activity. Elevated in haemolytic anaemia, acute blood loss, and post-treatment recovery. Low in aplastic anaemia and pure red cell aplasia. Differentiates hypoproliferative from hyperproliferative anaemias and monitors response to treatment.

name: Platelet Count
desc: Measures number of platelets per microlitre of blood. Thrombocytopenia (low platelets) is seen in dengue fever, ITP, DIC, and bone marrow suppression causing increased bleeding risk. Thrombocytosis occurs in iron deficiency anaemia, infection, and myeloproliferative disorders such as essential thrombocythaemia.

name: Prothrombin Time (PT / INR)
desc: Evaluates extrinsic and common coagulation pathway including factors I, II, V, VII, and X. Reported as INR to standardise results across laboratories. Used to monitor warfarin anticoagulant therapy, assess hepatic synthetic function in cirrhosis, and screen for bleeding disorders such as factor VII deficiency.

name: aPTT (Activated Partial Thromboplastin Time)
desc: Evaluates intrinsic coagulation pathway including factors VIII, IX, XI, and XII. Used to monitor unfractionated heparin therapy, diagnose haemophilia A (factor VIII deficiency) and haemophilia B (factor IX deficiency), and investigate lupus anticoagulant or antiphospholipid antibody syndrome.

name: D-Dimer
desc: Fibrin degradation product elevated when clots form and dissolve within blood vessels. Primary test to rule out deep vein thrombosis and pulmonary embolism in low-to-moderate probability patients. Also elevated in DIC, COVID-19 coagulopathy, sepsis, pregnancy, and post-surgical states requiring clinical correlation.

name: Fibrinogen Level
desc: Measures circulating fibrinogen, a clotting protein synthesised by the liver. Critically low in DIC, severe liver disease, and congenital hypofibrinogenaemia causing uncontrolled haemorrhage. Elevated fibrinogen is an independent cardiovascular risk factor and acute phase reactant in systemic inflammation and infection.

name: G6PD Enzyme Activity
desc: Measures Glucose-6-Phosphate Dehydrogenase enzyme activity in red blood cells. G6PD deficiency is the most common RBC enzyme disorder worldwide affecting approximately 400 million people. Causes episodic haemolytic anaemia triggered by oxidative stress from antimalarial drugs, nitrofurantoin, infections, or dietary fava beans.

name: Haemoglobin Electrophoresis (HPLC)
desc: Separates and quantifies haemoglobin variants (HbA, HbA2, HbF, HbS, HbC, HbD) using HPLC or electrophoresis. Essential for diagnosing thalassaemia trait with elevated HbA2, sickle cell disease with predominant HbS, and other haemoglobinopathies. Mandatory in antenatal screening and pre-marital counselling programmes.

name: Bleeding Time & Clotting Time
desc: Bleeding time assesses primary haemostasis by measuring time to cessation of bleeding from a standardised skin wound. Prolonged in thrombocytopenia, platelet function disorders, and von Willebrand disease. Clotting time evaluates overall coagulation. Used as initial pre-procedure screening before invasive interventions.

name: Malarial Antigen Rapid Test (PF/PV)
desc: Rapid antigen detection for Plasmodium falciparum (PfHRP2 antigen) and Plasmodium vivax (pLDH antigen) using immunochromatographic strip. WHO-recommended first-line test for febrile patients from endemic areas. Highly sensitive in active infection within first 5 days of fever. Confirm with blood smear for species identification.

name: Malaria Blood Smear (Thick & Thin)
desc: Gold standard for malaria diagnosis. Thick smear provides high sensitivity for parasite detection; thin smear enables species identification and parasitaemia quantification. Distinguishes P. falciparum, P. vivax, P. malariae, and P. ovale. Serial smears every 12 to 24 hours recommended if initial result is negative.

name: Dengue NS1 Antigen
desc: Detects dengue virus non-structural protein 1 present in blood during acute febrile phase from Day 1 to Day 5. Highly specific for early dengue diagnosis before antibodies develop. Best combined with dengue IgM and IgG serology for comprehensive coverage across all phases. Critical for timely platelet monitoring.

name: Dengue IgM & IgG Antibodies
desc: IgM antibodies appear from Day 5 to 7 indicating recent primary dengue infection. IgG indicates past exposure or secondary infection. Secondary IgG-positive infections carry significantly higher risk of dengue haemorrhagic fever and dengue shock syndrome due to antibody-dependent enhancement mechanism.

name: Typhoid IgM Rapid / Widal Test
desc: Detects agglutinating antibodies against Salmonella typhi somatic O antigen and flagellar H antigen. Widal titre above 1:160 for O antigen is clinically significant in non-endemic populations. IgM-specific rapid tests provide better early sensitivity. Must be interpreted alongside clinical features and local endemicity.

name: Blood Culture & Sensitivity
desc: Gold standard for diagnosing bacteraemia and fungaemia. Blood collected aseptically from two sites into automated culture bottles. Positive cultures undergo MALDI-TOF organism identification and Vitek-2 antibiotic sensitivity testing to guide targeted therapy and antibiotic stewardship in sepsis management.

name: Urine Culture & Sensitivity
desc: Cultures mid-stream urine to identify bacterial pathogens causing urinary tract infection. Significant bacteriuria defined as greater than 100,000 CFU/ml. Antibiotic sensitivity testing guides appropriate therapy, especially critical given rising ESBL-producing and carbapenem-resistant Enterobacteriaceae in community and hospital settings.

name: Throat Swab Culture
desc: Cultures throat secretions to detect Group A Streptococcus (Strep pyogenes) causing streptococcal pharyngitis. Untreated GAS throat infection can lead to acute rheumatic fever, rheumatic heart disease, and post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis. Also detects Klebsiella, Staphylococcus, Haemophilus, and Candida species.

name: Sputum Culture & Sensitivity
desc: Cultures deep expectorated sputum to identify lower respiratory tract pathogens causing community-acquired or hospital-acquired pneumonia. Organisms targeted include Streptococcus pneumoniae, Klebsiella pneumoniae, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, and Acinetobacter baumannii. AST guides targeted antibiotic selection.

name: AFB Smear & Culture (Tuberculosis)
sample: Sputum or BAL or Body Fluid
desc: AFB smear by Ziehl-Neelsen or Auramine O fluorescent staining provides rapid preliminary result. MGIT liquid culture is highly sensitive and allows complete drug susceptibility testing (DST) for first and second-line anti-TB drugs including rifampicin, isoniazid, and fluoroquinolones. Essential for MDR-TB detection.

name: Stool Culture & Sensitivity
desc: Cultures stool on selective media to isolate enteric pathogens causing infectious diarrhoea including Salmonella, Shigella, Campylobacter, Vibrio cholerae, and diarrhoeagenic E. coli. Antibiotic sensitivity guides therapy. Essential for outbreak investigation and management of severe or bloody diarrhoea.

name: Wound and Pus Culture & Sensitivity
desc: Cultures wound secretions or pus to identify causative organisms in surgical site infections, diabetic foot ulcers, burns, and abscesses. Commonly isolates Staphylococcus aureus including MRSA, Pseudomonas, E. coli, Klebsiella, and anaerobes. AST guides antibiotic therapy and guides surgical debridement decisions.

name: MRSA Screening (Nasal and Axilla Swab)
desc: Screens for Methicillin-Resistant Staphylococcus aureus colonisation in anterior nares and axillae. Critical for hospital infection control to identify carriers before elective surgeries and prevent nosocomial MRSA transmission. Colonised patients require mupirocin nasal decolonisation and chlorhexidine bathing before procedures.

name: KOH Preparation (Fungal Examination)
sample: Skin Scraping or Nail or Hair
desc: Potassium hydroxide wet mount preparation dissolves keratin to reveal fungal hyphae, arthroconidia, pseudohyphae, or spores under light microscopy. Diagnoses tinea corporis, tinea pedis, tinea unguium (onychomycosis), and cutaneous candidiasis rapidly. Cost-effective first-line investigation before antifungal initiation.

name: Gram Stain (Any Clinical Specimen)
sample: Wound Swab or CSF or Fluid or Sputum
desc: Rapid differential staining technique dividing bacteria into Gram-positive (crystal violet, purple) and Gram-negative (safranin, pink) based on cell wall structure. Provides preliminary organism identification and morphology within hours to guide empirical antibiotic selection while culture and sensitivity results are awaited.

name: Stool Routine Microscopy (Ova and Cyst)
desc: Detects intestinal parasites through direct microscopic examination. Identifies ova of Ascaris lumbricoides, hookworm, and Trichuris trichiura; cysts of Entamoeba histolytica and Giardia lamblia; and trophozoites in acute amoebic dysentery. Concentration techniques improve sensitivity for low-burden infections.

name: CSF Analysis (Routine + Culture)
desc: Comprehensive CSF analysis including appearance, opening pressure, cell count, differential, protein, glucose with simultaneous blood glucose, Gram stain, India ink stain for Cryptococcus, and culture. Differentiates bacterial meningitis (neutrophilic pleocytosis, low glucose, high protein) from viral, tuberculous, and fungal meningitis.

name: VDRL (Syphilis Screening)
desc: Non-treponemal flocculation test for syphilis screening using cardiolipin antigen. Reactive results require confirmation with specific treponemal tests such as TPHA or FTA-ABS. Quantitative VDRL titres are used to monitor treatment response, with a fourfold titre decline expected by 6 months post-adequate penicillin therapy.

name: TPHA (Treponemal Confirmatory Test)
desc: Specific confirmatory treponemal test for syphilis detecting antibodies against Treponema pallidum antigens. More specific than VDRL for syphilis confirmation. Remains reactive for life even after successful treatment reflecting past infection. Used to confirm reactive VDRL results and diagnose latent syphilis with negative non-treponemal tests.

name: HIV 1 and 2 Antibody with P24 Antigen (4th Gen)
desc: Fourth-generation combo ELISA simultaneously detects HIV-1 and HIV-2 antibodies and p24 antigen, reducing the diagnostic window period to approximately 2 to 3 weeks post-exposure. Reactive results require confirmatory Western blot or HIV RNA PCR. Mandatory test for blood donors, pregnant women, and pre-surgical patients.

name: HBsAg (Hepatitis B Surface Antigen)
desc: Earliest serological marker of HBV infection appearing 1 to 10 weeks after exposure, before clinical symptoms develop. Positive in both acute and chronic HBV infection. Chronic HBV defined as HBsAg positive beyond 6 months increases long-term risk of cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma requiring antiviral therapy.

name: Hepatitis B Core Antibody (Anti-HBc)
desc: Anti-HBc IgM indicates acute or recent HBV infection and is detectable during the window period when HBsAg has cleared but anti-HBs not yet appeared. Anti-HBc IgG persists lifelong as a marker of past infection. Total anti-HBc positive with surface antigen negative indicates resolved infection or occult hepatitis B.

name: Anti-HBs (Hepatitis B Surface Antibody)
desc: Measures protective antibody level following HBV vaccination or natural infection recovery. Level above 10 IU/L indicates protective immunity. Quantitative titres guide need for booster vaccine doses in healthcare workers, dialysis patients, and immunocompromised individuals where immunity may wane over time.

name: Anti-HCV (Hepatitis C Antibody)
desc: Screens for Hepatitis C virus antibodies. A reactive result indicates past or current infection requiring confirmatory HCV RNA PCR. Approximately 75 to 85% of acutely infected individuals develop chronic HCV leading to cirrhosis. Modern direct-acting antivirals achieve cure rates above 95% with 8 to 12 weeks of treatment.

name: Anti-HAV IgM (Hepatitis A Acute)
desc: Detects IgM antibodies against Hepatitis A virus indicating acute infection within past 3 to 6 months. HAV spreads via faecal-oral route through contaminated food and water. Causes self-limiting acute hepatitis with jaundice, nausea, malaise, and elevated transaminases. Fulminant hepatic failure occurs rarely but is life-threatening.

name: HEV IgM (Hepatitis E Acute)
desc: Detects IgM antibodies against Hepatitis E virus, important in South Asia and Africa. HEV genotype 1 causes epidemic waterborne hepatitis. Critically dangerous in pregnancy where it causes fulminant hepatic failure with up to 25% maternal mortality in the third trimester. Must be distinguished from HAV by specific serology.

name: RA Factor Quantitative (Rheumatoid Factor)
desc: Quantifies IgM antibodies directed against the Fc portion of IgG immunoglobulins. Positive in 70 to 80% of rheumatoid arthritis patients but also in Sjogren syndrome, SLE, mixed connective tissue disease, and chronic infections including hepatitis and endocarditis. Combined with anti-CCP for improved RA diagnostic specificity.

name: Anti-CCP Antibodies (Anti-Citrullinated Protein)
desc: Highly specific antibody exceeding 95% specificity for rheumatoid arthritis and detectable years before symptom onset. Predicts erosive joint disease and severe disease course. Guides early aggressive treatment with DMARDs such as methotrexate to prevent irreversible joint destruction. Superior diagnostic value compared to RA factor alone.

name: ANA by IFA (Antinuclear Antibody)
desc: Indirect immunofluorescence on HEp-2 cells detects antinuclear antibodies, the primary screening test for systemic autoimmune diseases. Positive in over 95% of SLE patients. Fluorescence patterns such as homogeneous, speckled, nucleolar, and centromere guide selection of specific antibody tests for further characterisation.

name: Anti-dsDNA Antibody (SLE Specific)
desc: Highly specific antibody for Systemic Lupus Erythematosus included in ACR and EULAR classification criteria. Elevated titres correlate with disease activity, lupus nephritis flares, and complement consumption. Serial monitoring guides immunosuppressive therapy decisions with hydroxychloroquine, steroids, and mycophenolate mofetil.

name: ASO Titre (Anti-Streptolysin O)
desc: Measures antibodies against streptolysin O produced by Group A Streptococcus. Elevated ASO titre above 200 IU per ml in adults confirms recent streptococcal infection. Used to diagnose post-streptococcal complications including acute rheumatic fever, rheumatic heart disease, and post-streptococcal acute glomerulonephritis.

name: CRP Quantitative (C-Reactive Protein)
desc: Sensitive acute-phase protein synthesised by the liver under IL-6 stimulation in response to inflammation, infection, or tissue injury. Quantitative CRP above 100 mg per L suggests bacterial infection or severe tissue damage. Used in sepsis workup, inflammatory condition monitoring, and post-operative infection surveillance.

name: Procalcitonin (PCT - Sepsis Marker)
desc: Superior biomarker for diagnosing bacterial sepsis and guiding antibiotic stewardship. PCT rises specifically in systemic bacterial infections within 2 to 4 hours reaching peak at 24 hours. Levels above 2 ng per ml indicate high likelihood of sepsis. Serial monitoring guides antibiotic duration and safe early discontinuation to prevent resistance.

name: Leptospira IgM Antibody
desc: Detects IgM antibodies against Leptospira interrogans, a spirochaetal zoonosis transmitted through contact with water contaminated by infected animal urine. Endemic in tropical regions during monsoon flooding. Presents with biphasic illness: leptospiraemic phase with fever and myalgia followed by immune phase with jaundice and renal failure (Weil disease).

name: Scrub Typhus IgM (Orientia tsutsugamushi)
desc: Detects IgM antibodies against Orientia tsutsugamushi transmitted by chigger mite bites. Endemic across South and Southeast Asia. Presents with fever, pathognomonic eschar at the bite site, regional lymphadenopathy, and maculopapular rash. Responds well to doxycycline 100 mg twice daily for 7 days if diagnosed promptly.

name: Chikungunya IgM Antibody
desc: Detects IgM antibodies against Chikungunya alphavirus transmitted by Aedes mosquitoes. Characterised by sudden fever and severe debilitating polyarthralgia affecting multiple joints simultaneously. IgM detectable from Day 5 of illness. Arthralgia can persist for months to years after acute illness in some patients.

name: H. pylori Antibody (IgG)
desc: Detects IgG antibodies against Helicobacter pylori, a gram-negative bacterium colonising the gastric mucosa. H. pylori is a WHO Class I carcinogen causing peptic ulcers, chronic gastritis, and gastric carcinoma. Serology cannot differentiate active from past infection; urea breath test or stool antigen test preferred for confirming active infection.

name: Urine Routine and Microscopy
desc: Complete physical, chemical, and microscopic urine analysis. Parameters include colour, clarity, specific gravity, pH, protein, glucose, ketones, bilirubin, urobilinogen, nitrites, and leucocyte esterase. Microscopy evaluates RBCs, WBCs, epithelial cells, casts (hyaline, granular, RBC, waxy), crystals, and yeast cells.

name: Blood Glucose Fasting (FBS)
desc: Plasma glucose after minimum 8-hour overnight fast. Normal 70 to 99 mg per dL. Impaired fasting glucose (prediabetes) 100 to 125 mg per dL. Diabetes mellitus confirmed at 126 mg per dL or above on two separate occasions per ADA guidelines. Fluoride tube prevents in vitro glycolysis ensuring accurate measurement.

name: Blood Glucose Post Prandial and Random
desc: Post-prandial glucose measured exactly 2 hours after a standard meal. Values at or above 200 mg per dL are diagnostic of diabetes. Random glucose at or above 200 mg per dL with symptoms also confirms diabetes. Used alongside fasting glucose for comprehensive glycaemic monitoring and gestational diabetes screening.

name: HbA1c (Glycosylated Haemoglobin)
desc: Reflects average blood glucose over 2 to 3 months by measuring percentage of glycosylated haemoglobin A1c. Normal below 5.7%. Prediabetes 5.7 to 6.4%. Diabetes 6.5% or above. Treatment target below 7% for most diabetics per ADA guidelines. Not affected by recent meals, fasting state, or time of day.

name: Serum Creatinine and eGFR
desc: Primary biomarker of renal filtration function. eGFR calculated using CKD-EPI or MDRD equation from creatinine, age, sex, and ethnicity. CKD staged G1 to G5 based on eGFR values. Approximately 50% reduction in GFR results in creatinine doubling due to the non-linear inverse relationship between eGFR and creatinine.

name: Blood Urea Nitrogen (BUN)
desc: Measures nitrogen component of urea, the major metabolic end-product of protein catabolism synthesised in the liver and excreted by kidneys. Elevated in acute kidney injury, CKD, dehydration, high protein intake, and upper GI bleeding. BUN to creatinine ratio above 20 to 1 suggests pre-renal azotaemia from dehydration or reduced perfusion.

name: Uric Acid
desc: Measures serum uric acid, the final oxidation product of purine metabolism via xanthine oxidase. Hyperuricaemia above 7 mg per dL in men and 6 mg per dL in women leads to monosodium urate crystal deposition causing gouty arthritis, tophi, and uric acid nephrolithiasis. Monitored during chemotherapy for tumour lysis syndrome risk.

name: Liver Function Test Complete Panel (LFT)
desc: Comprehensive hepatic panel including total protein, albumin, globulin, A:G ratio, total bilirubin, direct bilirubin, indirect bilirubin, AST (SGOT), ALT (SGPT), alkaline phosphatase (ALP), and GGT. Hepatocellular damage shows predominant transaminase elevation. Cholestatic pattern shows predominant ALP and GGT elevation.

name: Kidney Function Test Complete Panel (KFT)
desc: Comprehensive renal panel including blood urea, serum creatinine, eGFR, uric acid, sodium, potassium, chloride, bicarbonate, calcium, phosphate, and magnesium. Provides complete assessment of renal excretory function, electrolyte homeostasis, and acid-base balance. Essential for CKD staging and monitoring dialysis patients.

name: Lipid Profile Complete Panel
desc: Cardiovascular risk assessment panel measuring total cholesterol, HDL cholesterol, LDL cholesterol by calculation or direct measurement, VLDL, triglycerides, and non-HDL cholesterol after 10 to 12 hours fasting. Calculates atherogenic index and LDL to HDL ratio. Used to guide statin therapy decisions per ACC and AHA guidelines.

name: Thyroid Profile Complete (T3, T4, TSH)
desc: Measures total T3, total T4, and third-generation sensitive TSH. TSH is the most sensitive single indicator of thyroid function. Low TSH with high T3 and T4 indicates hyperthyroidism. High TSH with low T3 and T4 indicates hypothyroidism. Monitors thyroid hormone replacement therapy dosing and titration.

name: Electrolytes Complete (Na, K, Cl, HCO3)
desc: Measures sodium, potassium, chloride, and bicarbonate, the principal extracellular electrolytes governing osmolality and acid-base balance. Critical for managing hyponatraemia, life-threatening hyperkalaemia causing fatal arrhythmias, metabolic acidosis and alkalosis, and monitoring patients on diuretics, IV fluids, or ventilatory support.

name: Serum Calcium and Phosphate
desc: Calcium and phosphate are reciprocally regulated by PTH, calcitonin, and activated Vitamin D. Hypercalcaemia suggests hyperparathyroidism, malignancy, or sarcoidosis. Hypocalcaemia indicates hypoparathyroidism or Vitamin D deficiency. Hyperphosphataemia is a common complication of CKD and hypoparathyroidism.

name: Serum Iron, TIBC and Transferrin Saturation
desc: Serum iron measures circulating transferrin-bound iron. TIBC reflects total transferrin iron-binding capacity. Transferrin saturation equals serum iron divided by TIBC multiplied by 100. Low iron with high TIBC and saturation below 20% confirms iron deficiency. Saturation above 45% with low TIBC suggests iron overload or haemochromatosis.

name: Serum Ferritin
desc: Most reliable indicator of total body iron stores. Ferritin below 12 ng per mL confirms absolute iron deficiency. Elevated in haemochromatosis, haemolytic disorders, malignancy, severe liver disease, and inflammation as an acute phase reactant. Hyperferritinaemia above 500 ng per mL in macrophage activation syndrome is a critical finding.

name: Vitamin B12 (Cobalamin)
desc: Measures serum cobalamin essential for DNA synthesis, red blood cell maturation, myelin synthesis, and homocysteine remethylation. Deficiency causes megaloblastic macrocytic anaemia and subacute combined degeneration of the spinal cord with posterior and lateral column demyelination causing peripheral neuropathy and paraesthesia.

name: Vitamin D - 25 OH Total
desc: Measures 25-hydroxyvitamin D, the major circulating form and best indicator of overall Vitamin D status from sun exposure and dietary sources. Deficiency below 20 ng per mL causes rickets in children and osteomalacia in adults. Insufficiency 20 to 30 ng per mL associated with osteoporosis, muscle weakness, and increased infection risk.

name: Serum Amylase
desc: Digestive enzyme produced by the exocrine pancreas and salivary glands. Elevation above 3 times the upper limit of normal in acute pancreatitis and pancreatic duct obstruction. Rises within 2 to 12 hours of pancreatic injury and normalises within 3 to 5 days. Less specific than lipase for pancreatic disease due to salivary gland sources.

name: Serum Lipase
desc: Pancreatic-specific enzyme more sensitive and specific than amylase for acute pancreatitis. Elevation above 3 times the upper limit of normal is diagnostic per ACG guidelines. Remains elevated for 7 to 14 days providing a wider diagnostic window than amylase. Preferred marker when patients present late after onset of symptoms.

name: Total Bilirubin, Direct and Indirect
desc: Bilirubin fractionation classifies the mechanism of jaundice. Prehepatic haemolytic jaundice predominantly raises unconjugated indirect bilirubin. Hepatocellular jaundice raises both fractions. Post-hepatic obstructive cholestatic jaundice predominantly raises conjugated direct bilirubin alongside elevated ALP and GGT.

name: Serum Albumin
desc: Most abundant serum protein synthesised exclusively by the liver with a half-life of 20 days. Reflects hepatic synthetic function and nutritional status. Hypoalbuminaemia below 3.5 g per dL occurs in cirrhosis, nephrotic syndrome, malnutrition, protein-losing enteropathy, and severe catabolism. Used in Child-Pugh cirrhosis scoring.

name: High Sensitivity Troponin I or T (hs-cTn)
desc: Most sensitive and specific cardiac biomarker for myocardial injury. High-sensitivity troponin detects myocardial infarction within 1 to 3 hours of symptom onset. Serial measurements at 0 and 3 hours per ESC rapid rule-in and rule-out protocol. Essential for NSTEMI and acute coronary syndrome diagnosis in emergency settings.

name: CPK-MB (Creatine Phosphokinase MB Isoenzyme)
desc: Cardiac-specific isoenzyme of creatine kinase constituting 1 to 6% of total CK in cardiac muscle. Elevates within 3 to 6 hours of myocardial infarction, peaks at 12 to 24 hours, and normalises by 48 to 72 hours. Shorter duration than troponin allows detection of re-infarction. Used alongside troponin in acute coronary syndrome workup.
